description:
Hi! We are an enthusiastic team looking to solve challenges using open data and creative tech.
Our skills: Python, web development, data analysis, and space science fundamentals.
Who we're looking for: UI/UX designers, front-end developers, or researchers who enjoy turning complex datasets into practical, intuitive applications. Let’s collaborate and build something great!
summary: SkyBlink is a free web tool that lets anyone see how the sky changes in data from NASA's SPHEREx mission. Type a star name or coordinates, and SkyBlink fetches real SPHEREx spectral images from NASA/IPAC IRSA, groups them into visits months apart, aligns them on one sky grid and plays them as a blink animation, the technique that found Pluto in 1930. A Difference view turns a moving object into a black-and-white pair, and SkyBlink measures the shift in arcseconds, with an error checked against fixed field stars. Because SPHEREx's linear variable filters see each star at a different wavelength in every exposure, visits are compared inside a shared wavelength window and detectors are never mixed. On the challenge targets, it measures Epsilon Indi B moving 6.0 ± 1.1″ (catalogue 6.5″) and Barnard's Star 11.9 ± 1.3″ (catalogue 10.4″), and reports saturated or too-faint targets as such instead of inventing numbers. A wavelength slider, spectrum and light-curve previews, shareable links, an embeddable player, a findings feed and an English, Russian and Uzbek interface make SPHEREx usable for students and citizen scientists searching for brown dwarfs and other moving objects.
details:
What it does

SkyBlink is a free web app that brings the oldest trick in planet hunting, the "blink" that found Pluto in 1930, to NASA's newest infrared sky survey. Type a star name or coordinates (or open one of the five challenge targets) and SkyBlink shows real SPHEREx images of that patch of sky from different visits, aligned and played as an animation. Three views: Blink (visit by visit), Difference (a moving object becomes a black-and-white pair) and Deep sum (all exposures stacked to reveal faint sources). A wavelength slider steps through SPHEREx's six detectors from 0.75 to 5 µm: stars fade towards long wavelengths, while the cold brown dwarf WISE 0855−0714 appears only at the long end.

How it works

A Django backend queries NASA/IPAC IRSA (Simple Image Access v2, collections spherex_dr1 and spherex_qr3), downloads server-side cutouts, groups exposures into visits, reads the wavelength at the target for every exposure from the WCS-WAVE extension, masks bad and saturated pixels with the FLAGS layer, stacks each visit with inverse-variance weights, reprojects everything onto one sky grid with Astropy and reproject, and renders frames on one common brightness scale. A Next.js frontend plays the frames, draws "was" and "now" rings from catalogue proper motions, and links to an Aladin Lite sky map (AllWISE, 2MASS, DSS2).

Measured, not just shown

SPHEREx pixels are 6.15″, so nearby stars move about one pixel a year. SkyBlink therefore measures motion: flux-weighted centroids in the first and last visit give the shift in arcseconds, with an error that combines statistics and a registration check on fixed field stars. Results on real data: Epsilon Indi B 6.0 ± 1.1″ (catalogue 6.5″); Barnard's Star 11.9 ± 1.3″ with its saturated core masked (catalogue 10.4″, about 2σ, so indicative). Where an honest number is impossible, the app says so: WISE 0855 is too faint next to a background star, and RW Aurigae and R Draconis saturate SPHEREx, so their light curve and spectrum answer "saturated" instead of showing invented values.

Science layers

Click any pixel for a spectrum preview from 0.75 to 5 µm (with H₂O, CH₄, CO₂ and CO markers) and a light curve across visits, both measured on single real exposures and clearly labelled as previews. Gaia DR3 and CatWISE2020 positions (via IRSA TAP) are moved to the SPHEREx epoch and drawn as motion arrows when the catalogue service responds. A source that moves in the infrared but has no Gaia match is labelled "a candidate to check", never "a discovery".

Benefits and intended impact

Most known cold brown dwarfs near the Sun were confirmed with help from volunteers who blinked WISE images (Backyard Worlds: Planet 9). SkyBlink makes SPHEREx data usable in the same way, with no software to install and no FITS knowledge needed. Simple mode explains what you are looking at, a three-case trainer teaches how to tell real motion from a variable star or a detector artifact, and "I found something!" saves coordinates to a shared findings feed. The whole interface works in English, Russian and Uzbek, on desktop and phone. Every view has a shareable URL (?ra=&dec=&fov=&det=&mode=) and an embeddable player, so teachers and outreach sites can drop it into a page.

What makes it creative

SPHEREx's linear variable filters mean each pixel sees a different wavelength, so a naive blink shows colour changes as fake motion. SkyBlink compares visits only inside a shared wavelength window, never mixes detectors, and corrects coordinates to the epoch of their proper motion, which kept fast movers such as Barnard's Star and WISE 0855 inside the field. The 102-band survey becomes a slider that shows why cold objects appear only in the infrared.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty first: real data only, errors on every measurement, explicit limits (no parallax correction, previews labelled as previews, saturation reported). Speed for visitors: the five challenge targets are pre-computed and open in under a second, and new fields are downloaded from IRSA with polite limits (at most 4–6 parallel requests, retries with backoff). Accessibility: keyboard controls, reduced-motion support, three languages, mobile layout. Free hosting with a fallback: if the backend sleeps, the site still serves the five featured targets.

Tools

Python (Django, Django REST framework, Astropy, reproject, NumPy, Pillow, pytest), TypeScript (Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, next-intl, Zustand, Recharts, lucide-react), Aladin Lite v3, Render (backend), Vercel (frontend), GitHub. 81 backend tests and 9 frontend tests.

Team

Intizor (story and presentation), Makhmud (Core Viewer: blink engine, alignment, measured motion), Khayrulloh (Science Layers: catalogues, spectrum, light curve, sky map), Nizomiddin (Platform: search, presets, Simple mode, findings, three languages, deployment).

Not an official NASA product.
